title: Airtrunk tips data centre slowdown; Judo Bank’s SME bad loans rise
full_text:
That’s all from The Australian’s rolling coverage of business and markets news for Tuesday, October 20.
The big four lender is recognising a $41m pre-tax impact for expenses related to the RAMS litigation matters and associated legal costs.
The update comes ahead of its full year results update on November 2 – and follows Westpac’s completion of the sale of the $15.4bn RAMS mortgage portfolio to a consortium comprising Pepper Money, credit funds and accounts managed by KKR and PIMCO managed funds in August this year.
That transaction, entered into in November 2025, strengthened balance sheet and reduced operational complexity for Westpac – drawing to an end the saga that started with its Project Guardian investigation in 2022.
But it came after a $75m hit to the first half profit due to separation and transaction costs associated with the sale.
RAMS was closed to new business in August 2024 – after it was described as a hotbed of mortgage fraud. ASIC accused RAMS of writing liar loans, accepting fake pay slips and enabling the personal enrichment of branch staff across 84 incidents of systemic misconduct.
Disputes have been raised by franchisees who were exited by RAMS Financial Group, including the commencement of a class action in May 2024.
Westpac also paid a $20m penalty plus costs in October last year after civil penalty proceedings were agreed between financial regulator ASIC and RAMS in relation to RAMS’ oversight of conduct of third-party franchisees and franchisee employees who were authorised credit representatives between June 3, 2019 and April 30, 2023.
Westpac acquired the RAMS business in 2007 for $140m during the global financial crisis. At its peak, the portfolio represented nearly $31.8bn – or 3.7 per cent of Westpac’s total loan book.
Shares in Westpac last at $35.41.
